# Object Storage, CDN and Resource Distribution

## Category

database / cache subtree. Node position: object storage, CDN and resource distribution — developing addressing, versioning, permissions and refresh governance around the single goal of "letting the vast majority of reads never return to the origin".

## Definition


A client game's install packages, a mobile game's hot-update files, and the static assets of a launcher and official site all belong to the same class of problem: a large number of rarely changing files must be pulled quickly, cheaply and reliably by a massive number of users. Object storage is responsible for putting the files in place, and the CDN is responsible for moving the files close to the users. This layer is nearly invisible day to day, but once version management falls apart or cache policy goes out of control, the losses usually appear in the form of "an entire release fails" or "the bandwidth bill doubles".

## Problem

Resource distribution chases high throughput at low cost, and it cannot support the same architecture as a business interface's low latency and strong consistency; its errors are measured in "how many people failed to update", and losses often appear as an entire failed release or a doubled bandwidth bill. Publishing a new version over an old path leaves client, CDN and origin with long-term inconsistent content; treating cache refresh as a routine release step gets stuck on edge nodes still serving old content at rollback time.


### Why resource distribution is an independent layer of problem

Business interfaces chase low latency and strong consistency, resource distribution chases high throughput and low cost, and those two sets of goals cannot support the same architecture. Interfaces go through databases and cache, resources go through object storage and edge nodes; interface errors are counted in single-digit failed requests, while resource distribution errors are counted in "how many people failed to update".

What makes this layer special is:

- Files are large and numerous, and the cost of fetching a single file cannot be discussed on the same scale as an interface request.
- Reads are extremely numerous and writes extremely rare, with writes concentrated at the moment of release but reads stretching across the long time after the release.
- Users are widely distributed, and origin bandwidth plus cross-network traffic cost are far higher than business interface traffic.

So resource distribution design almost always revolves around one goal: let the vast majority of reads never return to the origin. Every subsequent discussion — addressing, versioning, refresh — is a projection of that goal at a different stage.

### Content addressing: let the file name carry its own version

What organizes files inside object storage directly determines how hard version management is. Overwriting a new version onto an old path is the easiest and also the most dangerous approach — for any client referencing that path, whether it gets the new file or the old one depends on which layer of cache along the way has not expired yet, and nobody can say.

A safer common practice is content addressing, so a new version naturally corresponds to a new path:

- Name by content hash, so changed content means a changed path, and the file is naturally immutable.
- Organize directories by version number or build number, so one release corresponds to a set of new objects.
- Manage a manifest file separately: the client fetches the manifest first, then fetches files by the paths listed in the manifest.

The value of an immutable path is turning "update" from overwrite-rewrite into a release: old and new versions coexist, you can always switch back when something breaks, and no layer of cache along the way has to be "persuaded". This immutability is the foundation for all the governance measures that follow.

### Version governance: rollback is switching a pointer, not re-uploading

The essence of a release is not "upload the new file", it is "declare some version to be the current version". Keep those two things apart and rollback is a pointer switch, done in seconds; blur them together and rollback is a re-upload plus an uncontrollable wait on the cache.

Version governance usually forms several disciplines:

- Keep each release's artifacts complete, rather than overwriting in place.
- Declare the current version with a separate, small, frequently changing manifest file.
- The client is compatible with multiple versions, and retiring an old version has an explicit time window.
- Generate both delta and full packages in advance, and verify them.

Games add one more dimension: channel packages. The same version often needs different packages for different channels, and if version number, channel number and build artifact do not line up, then when something breaks you cannot even answer "which version is actually running online". Whether version governance is competent shows exactly in whether it can produce an answer within minutes at such a moment.

### Permissions and hotlink protection: distribution does not mean public

Not all game assets should be public: paid content, test packages and embedded event materials all need access control. Object storage usually supports private read/write plus temporary authorization, and a CDN is often paired with validation parameters and domain control to restrict access.

Common control measures and their scope of applicability:

- Signed links with an expiry time, suitable for temporary distribution of test packages and paid content.
- Validation parameters, intercepting the outermost direct hotlinks at the lowest cost — but they do not stop someone who already has the link.
- Origin and domain whitelists, which can block crude off-site referencing; they are easy to forge, so treat them only as a first filter.

One point worth thinking through: once an asset has been downloaded by a client, a local copy exists, and no measure at the distribution layer can stop deliberate cracking. The goal of hotlink protection is to make casual, large-scale theft expensive, not to achieve strict secrecy — configure the strength of measures to that expectation, and overly heavy validation will instead hurt normal players' update experience.

### Cache refresh often cannot be relied on

The value of a CDN is caching files at edge nodes, and the cost is that "making the cache disappear" falls outside your control. After overwriting the origin file and issuing a refresh, it is usually only a signal: some nodes update, some keep the old content because they still hit the local cache, and the effective time differs unevenly across nodes.

Release paths that depend on refresh have their problems erupting in concentration at these moments:

- A canary wants to switch traffic by user, but the cache takes effect by file dimension, and the two curves do not line up.
- Something breaks and you need to roll back; the rollback package is pushed up, and edge nodes are still serving old files.
- The client has its own local cache layer, so a successful server-side refresh does not mean the user got the new version.

So the orientation at a mature team is usually the reverse: do not refresh by default, make paths immutable, and updating is releasing a new path. Refresh capability is kept, but only as an emergency tool, not a routine release step. Any scheme of "modify the old file and then wait for the cache to expire" will eventually become a troubleshooting nightmare at some version.

### The combination cost of multi-platform, multi-channel and hot update

The complexity of resource distribution is often not in a single file but in combinations: multiple languages, multiple device types, multiple channels and multiple versions online at the same time. What the manifest and delta mechanisms have to support is "each client computes its own set of files", not "everyone downloads the same package".

Questions usually worth answering in advance:

- How long does a hot update take from release until it takes effect for most players, and what happens on weak-network or low-storage devices.
- How many baseline versions do delta packages keep — too few and a delta degrades to a full package, too many and storage and management cost rise.
- What is the fallback path when the client's verification fails, and can it fall back to the previous usable version.

The answers to these questions together decide "how long after a release until the release can be called complete". The distribution layer's first-hand observation metrics are here too: player distribution across versions, hot-update success rate, delta hit rate — these predict the incoming support pressure better than the bandwidth curve.

### Common pitfalls

- Publishing a new version by overwriting an old path, leaving client, CDN and origin with long-term inconsistent content.
- Treating cache refresh as a routine step of the release process, and getting stuck on old edge-node content at rollback.
- Historical version artifacts are cleaned up or overwritten, so when something breaks even the files needed to reproduce the incident cannot be found.
- Assuming resources are safe once hotlink protection is configured, ignoring that the client's local copy is the real boundary.
- Watching only bandwidth cost and not monitoring player distribution across versions or hot-update success rate, so problems are only found on the support side.

The core judgment of the resource distribution layer is to understand a release as declaring a version rather than modifying files, and to understand refresh as an emergency means rather than a path you depend on.
